analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the requirement that federally funded highway and transit construction pay local prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let contractors pay lower wages on federally funded highway and transit projects, was referred to two House committees and died there without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires contractors on federally funded highway and public transportation projects to pay workers the wage that locally prevails for their trade — the standard set by the Davis-Bacon Act. This bill would repeal those requirements, letting contractors pay less than the local standard on such projects. It was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx with a handful of Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Education and Labor committees, and sent to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended [S1][S2][S3][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Construction firms that bid on federally funded highway and transit projects would gain, because wages are a major share of their bid costs; repealing the prevailing-wage rule would let them cut labor costs and bid lower. Taxpayers might see some projects cost the government less on paper, but the savings would come out of workers' paychecks.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sections of federal law (23 U.S.C. 113 and 49 U.S.C. 5333(a)) that require locally prevailing wages for laborers and mechanics on federal-aid highway and public transportation construction projects [S2][S3].
Existing contracts and bids already outstanding when the bill took effect would have been unaffected; the change would apply only to contracts signed after the 31st day following enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded highway and transit projects would bear the cost, since the local prevailing-wage floor on their pay would disappear. Studies of Davis-Bacon generally find that wages and benefits on covered projects fall when the requirement is removed, particularly for less-skilled workers.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the wage floor would directly reduce pay for the laborers and mechanics the bill covers; that is the mechanism by which contractors' costs drop [S2][S3].

A good-faith supporter would acknowledge that prevailing-wage rules also underpin local wage standards and union-scale training and benefits in the trades; removing them on federal projects could pull down standards those workers rely on, even where it lowers bids.

Supporters argue prevailing-wage rules inflate the cost taxpayers pay for construction; an honest weighing must note the tradeoff, but the bill's design put the entire burden of any savings on one group of workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts money from construction workers to contractors on federally funded projects. Any savings to the federal government from lower bids come entirely out of workers' wages, and there is no provision protecting or compensating the affected workers. It is a straightforward transfer with no balancing benefit for the people who would pay for it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to the Highways and Transit Subcommittee, and no committee or chamber vote ever happened before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC) introduced the bill on January 26, 2009, with four original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee [S1][S3][S5].
Nine Republicans in total cosponsored the bill [S4].
On January 27, 2009, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, and no further action was taken for the rest of the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers on federally funded highway and transit projects are better off because the bill died: their prevailing-wage floor remained in place, and contractors never got the lower labor costs the bill would have granted them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Construction workers, who kept wage floor

for.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
for.role: Sponsor, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal prevailing-wage requirements on federal-aid highway and transit construction projects [S1][S3].

against.name: Rep. James Oberstar
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or floor vote after it was referred to his committee [S5].

against.name: Rep. George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration in the second committee of referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Republicans in a Democratic-controlled House; no Democrat supported it in the record, and the Democratic committee chairs never brought it up [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would let contractors cut labor costs on federally funded projects by paying below the local prevailing wage. Their gain comes directly out of the pay of the workers on those projects.

industries.industry: Construction workers and building trades unions
industries.note: The wage floor these workers rely on for federal project pay would be repealed. Unions and prevailing-wage defenders would lose a core protection they have long defended.
